video_title: Scott Ramsower: Continuation Vehicles from the LP Seat
gist: Scott Ramsower, head of private equity funds at the $250B Teacher Retirement System of Texas and ILPA board chair, lays out a top-10 list of why LPs distrust GP-led continuation vehicles (conflicted pricing, fee step-ups via higher cost basis, synthetic DPI, lost right-tail upside, co-invest cannibalization, industry-wide return drag) and how TRS handles them. He also warns that 2018-2022 vintages face a structural DPI problem that will spawn zombie funds CVs cannot fix, argues retail PE is 'the right strategy but the wrong structure', and describes deeper underwriting of unrealized NAV and GP partnership cohesion.

insights.claim: LP sentiment toward GP-led continuation vehicles has hit new lows, with senior LPs calling them 'conflict vehicles' and some saying CVs could be the death of the private equity industry, while GPs initially celebrated them as a fourth exit route alongside IPO, sponsor sale and strategic sale.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: A GP-LP rift over the fastest-growing exit channel signals coming pushback on terms, approvals and CV volume, relevant to secondaries managers and listed alt managers.
insights.quote: There's a joke now that CV stands for conflict vehicle. Some LPs say my heart sinks when a CV request lands in my inbox.

insights.claim: In a continuation vehicle the GP sits on both sides of the trade, acting as agent for the selling legacy LPs and functionally for the incoming CV buyers, making it hard to know whether the price is real or a competitive process was run.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Structural price-discovery weakness means CV marks and exit prices should be treated skeptically by both sellers and buyers.
insights.quote: The GP sits on both sides of the trade.

insights.claim: ILPA is drafting a 2.0 version of its continuation vehicle best practices built on four pillars: rationale (CV as deliberate solution vs default), process (truly competitive auction including non-secondary buyers and a wholesale sale attempt), pricing support (bid transparency plus third-party fairness opinion), and governance/alignment (review time, economic neutrality, GP rolling its carry).
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Upcoming ILPA standards will shape CV process costs and timelines, likely lengthening deals and raising the bar for GP-led secondaries.

insights.claim: LPs are now demanding visibility into the full slate of final CV bids because a bidder offering 89 cents on the dollar plus a commitment to the GP's next fund may be chosen over one offering 90 cents, a side benefit LPACs typically do not disclose.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Bundling of primary commitments into CV bids is a hidden GP benefit; expect disclosure requirements that could compress secondary buyers' ability to win via fundraising sweeteners.
insights.quote: one bidder is willing to pay 90 cents on the dollar for an asset, another bidder will pay 89 cents on the dollar, but commit to the GP's next fund

insights.claim: Third-party fairness opinions on CV pricing are viewed by many LPs as having limited value, serving more as a process check than true valuation validation.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Fairness opinions should not be relied on as price evidence when evaluating CV roll-or-sell decisions.

insights.claim: Evaluating a CV is like a co-investment (form a view on the asset) plus an extra step co-invests rarely need: determining where the GP's alignment lies, since unlike a co-invest the GP is not buying and selling on the same terms as the LP.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: CV underwriting is more resource-intensive than co-invest, favoring large LPs with dedicated teams.

insights.claim: Rolling LPs in a CV can pay more for the same asset because the management fee resets on a stepped-up cost basis: a 70bp CV fee on an asset marked to $300 costs more than the original fund's 100bp post-investment-period fee on the $100 original cost, and tiered carry can exceed the original fund's carry.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Headline CV fee cuts can mask fee increases; LPs should compute dollar fees on new basis and demand 'economic status quo'.
insights.quote: LP is now paying 70 basis points on $300, which is higher than 100 basis points on $100.

insights.claim: CVs create a new fee and carry stream that lets the GP win even when the original fund loses, diluting the alignment LPs seek, and every hour a GP spends on a CV also dilutes mindshare from the commingled fund.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: GP-level economics from CVs can decouple from flagship fund performance, a misalignment risk for LPs and a revenue tailwind for GPs.
insights.quote: This opens the door for the GP to win even if the original fund loses.

insights.claim: Although CVs are framed as a free roll-or-sell choice, many LPs effectively must sell because board approvals, legal review and bandwidth cannot fit within election windows that are often only 20 to 30 business days.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Short election windows systematically push supply to secondary buyers, supporting their deal flow and pricing power.
insights.quote: While it's presented as a choice, a lot of LPs don't have a choice. As a result, their only option is to sell.

insights.claim: Selling an asset into a CV locks in DPI and IRR for the original fund even though value creation is ongoing, inflating GP track records; TRS shows its investment committee both actual DPI and DPI excluding 'synthetic DPI' from CVs and NAV loans.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Reported DPI across the industry may overstate real liquidity; strip CV and NAV-loan distributions when comparing managers.
insights.quote: we call it synthetic DPI when it's a CV or an NAV loan. We'll strip all of that out.

insights.claim: LPs pay 2-and-20 for three GP functions (sourcing, value creation, exit), and a GP that pushes assets into CVs abdicates the exit decision to LPs without any fee reduction, making limited partners 'less limited'.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: A latent argument for fee renegotiation, though he admits the 2-and-20 infrastructure makes near-term change unlikely.
insights.quote: us limited partners are becoming less limited. We're not paying any less

insights.claim: CVs cannibalize fee-free co-investment: assets that would have been sold to another (often too-small) sponsor requiring no-fee, no-carry co-invest now go into fee-paying CVs, and existing co-investors are forced to either exit or roll into full fees and full carry.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: LP co-invest pipelines shrink while GP fee-bearing AUM grows, shifting economics from LPs to GPs.

insights.claim: CVs are often created when an asset reaches 3x to 10x in the fund and are typically underwritten to at least another 2x, so an asset sold at 5x that would have become a 10x in the original fund has its right tail transferred to CV buyers.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Legacy LPs who sell forfeit the skewed outlier returns that justify PE; CV buyers capture them.
insights.quote: This is an asset that was sold at a 5x out of the fund is being underwritten at a 2x in a CV. Had that stayed in the original fund, that would have been a 10x deal.

insights.claim: Systematically moving the best assets out of commingled funds into CVs before final exit could exert downward pressure on private equity returns industry-wide, especially as data suggest LPs sell more than they roll.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Future commingled-fund return benchmarks may underperform history as winners are siphoned into CVs; secondary buyers may be the relative beneficiaries.
insights.quote: CVs could have downward pressure on private equity returns industry wide.

insights.claim: CV returns are self-limiting: if CVs perform too well LPs will stop letting GPs sell out of original funds (too-cheap pricing), and if too poorly LPs stop funding CV buyers, so the subsector structurally cannot be too good or too bad; early data he has seen supports this.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Expect CV strategy returns to cluster near market rather than deliver persistent outperformance, tempering enthusiasm for dedicated CV funds.
insights.quote: CVs by their nature can't be structurally too good, also can't be structurally too bad.

insights.claim: Presenting a GP's CV track record to an investment committee is a no-win: strong CV returns imply the asset was sold too cheaply, while weak ones imply poor judgment in keeping it.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: CV-heavy GPs may face harder re-ups with institutional committees regardless of outcomes.
insights.quote: There's not a CV track record that can win in terms of an investment committee.

insights.claim: Teacher Retirement System of Texas sits on the advisory board of almost every fund it invests in and uses an internal scorecard to decide on waiving CV conflicts, voting no if the GP has not met its criteria.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Large LPs are institutionalizing CV gatekeeping, raising approval risk for GPs that skip best practices.

insights.claim: TRS only does full roll-or-sell diligence on CVs above a size threshold, and its hit rate on CV rolls roughly matches its co-invest hit rate of about one in ten, reflecting no house view that CVs are inherently good or bad.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Even a sophisticated LP rolls only around 10% of CVs it evaluates, implying most legacy stakes flow to secondary buyers.
insights.quote: If we do one out of 10 co-invest, we probably do one out of 10 rolls.

insights.claim: TRS's co-investment team has opened itself up as a buyer of third-party CVs beyond its own roll decisions, applying a higher bar because CVs carry fees versus its typical no-fee, no-carry co-invest flow.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Large pensions entering as direct CV buyers adds capital competition for dedicated secondaries funds.

insights.claim: A Coller ('Caller' in transcript) survey this summer found 54% of LPs expect more zombie funds in their portfolios two years from now, up from 28% two years ago.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: A near-doubling in expected zombie funds signals mounting stranded NAV and governance burdens across LP portfolios.
insights.quote: 54% of LPs expect the number of zombie funds in their portfolio two years from now to be higher. Two years ago, that number was 28%.

insights.claim: The 2018-2022 vintages deployed capital in a low-rate, high-multiple environment that no longer exists, so exit math doesn't work and a structural DPI problem will take years to work through.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Expect prolonged low distributions, LP-interest discounts and pressure on fundraising for managers with heavy 2018-2022 exposure.
insights.quote: The math doesn't work on exits. As a result, there's a structural DPI problem.

insights.claim: CVs will not solve the zombie fund problem because there are far more stranded assets than CV capital; they merely kick the can down the road for individual assets or GPs.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Secondary capital supply is insufficient for the backlog, supporting wide secondary discounts and buyer-favorable pricing.
insights.quote: There's far more stranded assets than there is capital for CVs.

insights.claim: Zombie fund GPs keep collecting fees on NAV or cost basis with little incentive to force sales because they may be out of the carry, leaving trapped cash that can only exit via secondaries at significant discounts.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Misaligned fee incentives prolong zombie funds; LPs may need to push for fee step-downs or sell at discounts.

insights.claim: Outside a couple of large growth-capital names, the IPO market has seen little PE exit activity, and TRS is not encouraging GPs to exit via IPO because it is only step one of a multi-step exit with rarely full day-one liquidity.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Do not count on an IPO window to clear the PE backlog; sponsor-to-sponsor and secondaries remain the main routes.
insights.quote: I call an IPO step one of a multi-step exit

insights.claim: Private equity for retail investors is 'the right strategy but the wrong structure': semi-liquid quarterly-redemption vehicles remove the long-term horizon that is PE's advantage, since illiquidity is a feature, not a bug.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Institutional LP skepticism of evergreen/semi-liquid wrappers is a headwind narrative for retail-focused alt-manager growth stories.
insights.quote: private equity for the retail investor is the right strategy but the wrong structure

insights.claim: Institutional LPs are scrutinizing LPAs for hard caps on how much a retail vehicle can invest alongside a commingled fund, since uncapped sharing effectively turns a $10 billion fund into an uncapped one, plus buy/sell timing rules between retail and institutional vehicles and co-invest cannibalization.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Expect negotiated sharing caps and allocation rules that could constrain how fast GPs scale retail sleeves on flagship deals.
insights.quote: If that LPA allows a retail vehicle to invest infinite amounts, then I've effectively signed up for an uncapped fund.

insights.claim: Retail PE activity is so far concentrated among large public alternative asset managers, but eventually they will want middle-market offerings and distribution, likely driving joint ventures and consolidation where big GPs buy smaller ones.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: A consolidation catalyst for mid-market GPs and an M&A angle for listed alt managers.
insights.quote: you may see consolidation of GPs, you may see the big buying the smaller

insights.claim: A CEO of a large publicly traded alternative manager told him he was glad to run a large firm rather than a small one right now because of the strength of consolidation.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Scale advantages are perceived by industry leaders themselves, supporting the large-manager consolidation thesis.
insights.quote: I'm glad I'm CEO of a large firm and not a small firm right now

insights.claim: TRS now underwrites GPs' unrealized portfolios far more deeply, examining entry multiples, EBITDA and revenue since entry, actual vs budget by asset, current leverage, where portfolio companies' credits trade, and secondary bids for LP interests, because assuming a deal at cost will reach 2x no longer holds.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Using public credit pricing and secondary bids as cross-checks on NAV is a practical method to detect stale marks.
insights.quote: We've even gone out and looked at where are the portfolio's credits trading?

insights.claim: Many PE partnerships formed during the past 10-15 good years have never been tested, and cracks tend to appear when deals underperform, carry isn't paid, the next fund is smaller or layoffs start, so TRS is spending more diligence on partnership cohesion via reference calls, departures and full-day on-sites.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Expect rising GP team breakups in a low-carry environment; team stability becomes a key re-up risk factor.
insights.quote: A lot of these partnerships haven't been tested.

insights.claim: TRS uses a return-vs-risk matrix: it leans into high-risk managers only if they are 'n of one' with irreplicable returns, and passes on high-risk managers whose return stream can be recreated elsewhere with less risk.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Undifferentiated managers with key-person or strategy-drift risk face the toughest fundraising from large LPs.

insights.claim: TRS's private equity program grew from 6 people and about $7 billion NAV to 27 professionals and about $33 billion, but future alpha will come from 'craftsmanship alpha' (refining processes, more sourcing, AI tools) rather than new markets; secondaries are not a team-build focus and no new geographic offices beyond London are planned.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: A mature mega-LP signals evolutionary rather than expansionary growth, implying steady rather than rising PE allocations.
insights.quote: it's now all about craftsmanship alpha

insights.claim: Having invested through the GFC, he concluded that when others pull back you should go in, citing 2009 and 2010 as incredible PE vintages.
insights.speaker: Scott Ramsower
insights.so_what: Implies dislocated periods like today's liquidity drought may produce strong vintages for LPs who keep deploying.
insights.quote: when others are pulling back, go in. 2009 ended up being an incredible vintage.
